capability_descriptions.text: Answering questions, summarising and pulling facts from documents, everyday writing.
capability_descriptions.coding-agent: Fixing and changing real software on its own, checked by each project's tests.
capability_descriptions.tool-use: Calling office tools: create a document, send an email, look up a client.
capability_descriptions.speaker-labelling: Tagging each line of a transcript with who said it.
capability_descriptions.voice-output: Reading text aloud in a natural voice (narration).
capability_descriptions.images: Generating and editing pictures from a description.
capability_descriptions.memory: Keeping an assistant's notes about a person up to date without inventing or keeping rejected facts.
capability_descriptions.fine-tuning: Training a model on the box on your own examples.

capability_frontier.text: Level with Anthropic's models on routine document work; clearly behind on client drafting.
capability_frontier.coding-agent: Level with Claude on everyday and medium fixes, much slower; Claude solved all ten large changes, the local model half.
capability_frontier.tool-use: Not compared with a frontier model yet.
capability_frontier.speech-to-text: Not compared with a frontier service yet.
capability_frontier.speaker-labelling: Not compared with a frontier service yet.
capability_frontier.voice-output: Not compared with a frontier service yet.
capability_frontier.images: Not compared with a frontier service yet.
capability_frontier.music: Not compared with a frontier service yet.
capability_frontier.memory: Not compared with a frontier model yet.
capability_frontier.fine-tuning: Not comparable: frontier models cannot be trained on this machine.

halogen.name: Halogen
halogen.why: Fastest of five engines on production's model (86 tok/s on code, 18.7 s to first word at 32K, 4 Nov); closed source.
halogen.why_plain: Made by Peonist. It runs my everyday model and was the fastest of five engines I tested.
halogen.description_plain: Peonist LLC sells this engine and keeps its code closed. It runs my everyday model in Peonist's own compressed format, tuned for this chip.
halogen.strengths_plain: The fastest of five engines on my everyday model: 86 tokens a second on code, and 18.7s to start on a long document.
halogen.limits_plain: Closed source. It runs one model at a time. Its route for other model files would not start beside my speech service.

htr-vllm.name: HTR backup engine
htr-vllm.why: Community build of vLLM with its own compression: similar coding results to production (6/10 vs 5/10), about 25% slower writing.
htr-vllm.why_plain: My backup engine. It's about a quarter slower, with similar results on my coding test.
htr-vllm.description_plain: HawgAuto's fork of vLLM, the engine many cloud services are built on. It serves a copy of my everyday model shrunk by the HTR compression method.
htr-vllm.strengths_plain: Similar results on my coding test: 6 of 10 large changes against Halogen's 5.
htr-vllm.limits_plain: Slower: 47.8 against 62.5 tokens a second when writing, and about 1.6 times longer to read a long document.

loom.name: AMD Loom
loom.why: AMD's engine in development: 2.7 times llama.cpp on long prompts, but not faster than Halogen.
loom.why_plain: Reads long documents as fast as Halogen but writes more slowly; AMD is still building it.
loom.description_plain: AMD is building Loom for its own chips, and it is not finished yet.
loom.strengths_plain: Reads long documents about 2.7 times faster than llama.cpp, about level with the everyday engine.
loom.limits_plain: Writes more slowly than the everyday engine. It is a development release.

llama.cpp.name: llama.cpp
llama.cpp.why: The open-source standard; runs almost any model, so most model tests use it. About a third of Halogen's speed on production's model.
llama.cpp.why_plain: Nearly every new model runs on it within days, so I test most models here first; about a third of Halogen's speed.
llama.cpp.description_plain: Most people who run models at home start here. It is open source and supports almost every model soon after release.
llama.cpp.strengths_plain: Runs nearly every model I try, usually within days of release.
llama.cpp.limits_plain: About a third of Halogen's speed on my everyday model.

talus.name: Talus
talus.why: Community engine for this chip: 2.5 times llama.cpp on code; runs the 27B runner-up.
talus.why_plain: Runs my dense runner-up model at about 2.5 times llama.cpp's speed on code. Written for this chip alone.
talus.description_plain: Talus is a small community project made only for this chip. I used it for the dense runner-up model, Qwen3.8-27B.
talus.strengths_plain: About 2.5 times llama.cpp's speed on code.
talus.limits_plain: Slower than Halogen on my everyday model.

gufo.name: gufo
gufo.why: Community engine: second fastest on code in the 4 Nov comparison.
gufo.why_plain: Came second only to Halogen on code in my November speed test, and arrives as a ready-made container.
gufo.description_plain: Comes as a ready-to-run container from the gufo-org project. I tested it once, for speed, on my everyday model.
gufo.strengths_plain: Second fastest of five engines on code with my everyday model.
gufo.limits_plain: Tested for speed only, not for answer quality.

strata.name: Strata
strata.why: Community engine (MIT): 2.2 times llama.cpp on code; ran Hy4-Flash.
strata.why_plain: Loaded a 220B model, though that model was too slow here for long coding jobs. MIT-licensed.
strata.description_plain: Niko1221's open-source engine for this chip. It is the engine I used for the 220B Hy4-Flash model.
strata.strengths_plain: About 2.2 times llama.cpp's speed on code. It also ran a very large 220B model here.
strata.limits_plain: That large model was too slow for long coding jobs here, about 24 tokens a second.

atlas.name: Atlas
atlas.why: Community engine: about 27% faster than llama.cpp here; one mode unusable.
atlas.why_plain: About 27% faster than llama.cpp in my test on a standard agent workload.
atlas.description_plain: A community engine for this chip from Avarok, licensed AGPL. I measured it on a standard agent workload in September.
atlas.strengths_plain: About 27% faster than llama.cpp on a standard agent workload.
atlas.limits_plain: Its results vary slightly from run to run.

ciru.name: CIRU runtime
ciru.why: Community vLLM packaging for this chip; ran Inkling-2-Mini.
ciru.why_plain: Gave Inkling-2-Mini its draft model and a 2 to 2.5 times speed-up. One developer's packaging of vLLM for this chip.
ciru.description_plain: jcbtc packaged vLLM and AMD's libraries so they run on this chip. I used it for one model, Inkling-2-Mini, with its matching draft model.
ciru.strengths_plain: Runs Inkling-2-Mini with its matching draft model, about 2 to 2.5 times faster than without it.
ciru.limits_plain: I tested it on one model only.

whisper.cpp.name: whisper.cpp
whisper.cpp.why_plain: Transcribes a clean recording about 28 times faster than real time. All my call transcription goes through it.
whisper.cpp.description_plain: A C++ port of OpenAI's Whisper speech model that runs on ordinary hardware. Every call I record is transcribed with it on this machine.
whisper.cpp.strengths_plain: About 28 times faster than real time on a clean recording, with 2.4% of words wrong on a standard test.
whisper.cpp.limits_plain: It invents words in long silences unless voice detection runs first, as it does in my setup.

wespeaker.name: WeSpeaker + Silero
wespeaker.why_plain: Tells my voice from my guests' on 97% of lines, with voice detection running first.
wespeaker.description_plain: WeSpeaker is a research toolkit for recognising voices; I use its published voice model. Silero voice detection runs first, so silence is skipped.
wespeaker.strengths_plain: Labelled 97% of lines correctly as host or other on four real calls.
wespeaker.limits_plain: It tells the host from everyone else; it does not name each guest.

pyannote.name: pyannote
pyannote.why: Better general diarisation, slower; not needed for host-or-other.
pyannote.why_plain: Better at separating many speakers, slower, and more than I need for host or guest.
pyannote.description_plain: Researchers widely use this toolkit to work out who spoke when. I tried it beside my simpler approach in July.
pyannote.strengths_plain: Better at separating many speakers than my host-or-guest approach.
pyannote.limits_plain: Slower, and not needed when the job is host or other.

chatterbox.name: Chatterbox
chatterbox.why_plain: Reads my articles aloud in a cloned British female voice. Resemble AI's voice-copying engine.
chatterbox.description_plain: Resemble AI publishes this voice engine under the MIT licence. Give it a short, clean sample and it speaks in that voice.
chatterbox.strengths_plain: Won my voice tests for natural narration.
chatterbox.limits_plain: Needs a clean reference clip for the voice it copies.

kokoro.name: Kokoro
kokoro.why: Fixed voices; the opt-in narration fallback.
kokoro.why_plain: Small and fast, with fixed built-in voices; it narrates when the cloned voice is off.
kokoro.description_plain: A small text-to-speech model, run here through the kokoro-onnx package. It has built-in voices and needs no voice sample.
kokoro.strengths_plain: Fast and clear, with a built-in British female voice.
kokoro.limits_plain: Fixed voices only; it cannot copy a voice.

sd.cpp.name: stable-diffusion.cpp
sd.cpp.why_plain: Makes my everyday pictures in seconds, without a heavy Python stack.
sd.cpp.description_plain: This C++ engine runs image models on ordinary hardware. My everyday image model, FLUX.1-schnell, runs on it.
sd.cpp.strengths_plain: Makes usable images in seconds on this machine.
sd.cpp.limits_plain: I have not compared its image quality in depth.

diffusers.name: diffusers on ROCm PyTorch
diffusers.why: Runs Qwen-Image-2.1, only with the gateway down.
diffusers.why_plain: Runs the stronger Qwen-Image-2.1 model, but only with the whole machine to itself.
diffusers.description_plain: Hugging Face maintains this Python library, the usual way researchers run image models. I used it for the larger Qwen-Image-2.1.
diffusers.strengths_plain: Runs a stronger image model than my everyday one.
diffusers.limits_plain: Needs the whole machine, so it runs only when nothing else is serving.

audio.cpp.name: audio.cpp
audio.cpp.why: Runs the three song models tested.
audio.cpp.why_plain: Made a two-minute song in about 95s with ACE-Step, the only fast song model I tried.
audio.cpp.description_plain: This engine runs music models in C++, shipped as ready-made packages. I tried three song generators on it in November.
audio.cpp.strengths_plain: ACE-Step made songs faster than real time; the other two were much slower.
audio.cpp.limits_plain: No model here matched the musical style I wanted.

cloud-api.name: cloud API
cloud-api.why: Cloud models used as comparisons and judges only.
cloud-api.why_plain: Clearly better at client drafts and large software changes, but your data leaves the building and every call is paid for.
cloud-api.description_plain: Frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI and others, reached over the internet. I use them to compare and to judge, never for everyday work.
cloud-api.strengths_plain: Clearly better at client drafting and large software changes.
cloud-api.limits_plain: Your data leaves the building, and every call is paid for.

setups.reason_plain: Best local result on my coding tests and fast on everyday office work.
